# Benign prostatic hyperplasia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Urologic surgery > Benign prostatic hyperplasia*

[Original Article Link](/library/pi0Lsf)

---

## Summary

Benign <u>prostatic</u> <u>hyperplasia</u> (BPH) is a nonneoplastic glandular and stromal <u>hyperplasia</u> of the transition zone of the <u>prostate</u>. It is a common disorder, affecting ∼ 40% of the male population by the age of 50 years. Although the underlying etiology of BPH has not been conclusively established, sex <u>hormones</u> likely play a key role. BPH typically manifests as <u>lower urinary tract symptoms</u> (<u>LUTS</u>), which includes features of <u>bladder</u> irritation (<u>urinary frequency</u>, urgency, <u>urge incontinence</u>), features of <u>bladder outlet obstruction</u> (urinary hesitancy, straining to urinate, sensation of incomplete voiding), and <u>hematuria</u>. The initial workup comprises standardized questionnaires to assess symptom severity, <u>physical examination</u> including <u>digital rectal examination</u> (<u>DRE</u>), <u>urinalysis</u>, a <u>voiding diary</u>, and, in select patients, serum <u>prostate-specific antigen</u> (<u>PSA</u>) analysis. <u>DRE</u> may reveal a smooth, enlarged, nontender, and firm <u>prostate</u>. Imaging and <u>urodynamic studies</u> are indicated in patients with <u>features of complicated LUTS</u> and to guide management. Behavioral modifications (e.g., fluid restriction at night, <u>bladder training</u>) are advised in all patients with <u>LUTS</u> caused by BPH and may be the only management required in patients with minimal symptoms. Pharmacotherapy, such as <u>alpha blockers</u>, <u>5-alpha reductase inhibitors</u> (<u>5-ARIs</u>), and <u>parasympatholytics</u>, for BPH is indicated in patients with bothersome symptoms; the choice of agent depends on the size of the <u>prostate</u> and the predominant symptoms. <u>Surgery</u>, e.g., <u>transurethral resection of the prostate</u> (<u>TURP</u>), is indicated in patients with severely symptomatic BPH, those with complications due to BPH (e.g., <u>urinary retention</u>, <u>recurrent UTIs</u>, <u>hydroureteronephrosis</u>), and those who experience intolerable adverse effects with pharmacotherapy. In patients with BPH, the risk of developing <u>prostate cancer</u> is not higher than that of the general male population; therefore, standard <u>PSA</u> screening protocol can be followed. <u>TURP</u> does not reduce the risk of developing <u>prostate cancer</u> and, following the procedure, BPH recurs in ∼ 7% of men.

---

## Definitions

* Benign <u>prostatic</u> <u>hyperplasia</u> (BPH): benign glandular and stromal <u>hyperplasia</u> of the transitional zone of the <u>prostate</u>

* Benign prostatic syndrome (<u>BPS</u>): <u>lower urinary tract symptoms</u> caused by benign <u>hyperplasia</u> of the transitional zone of the <u>prostate</u>

* <u>Bladder outlet obstruction</u> (<u>BOO</u>): any obstruction to urinary outflow from the <u>bladder</u> which presents with <u>lower urinary tract symptoms</u> and is confirmed on <u>urodynamic testing</u> (see “<u>Lower urinary tract obstruction</u>” for causes of <u>BOO</u>)

* Benign prostatic obstruction (<u>BPO</u>): <u>BOO</u> caused by BPH

## Epidemiology

<u>Prevalence</u> of BPH increases with age (present in ∼ 50% of men > 50 years and more than 80% of men > 80 years). [[1]](/library/0PbeWF)



Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The etiology is not fully understood. The following factors play a role in <u>prostatic</u> <u>hyperplasia</u> and growth:




* Hormonal factors

* <u>Androgens</u>

* <u>Dihydrotestosterone</u> (<u>DHT</u>) is a potent <u>prostatic</u> growth factor.

* <u>Gene amplification</u> of <u>androgen</u> <u>receptors</u> (present in the glandular <u>epithelial</u> cells and stromal cells) → increased <u>androgen</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>sensitivity</u> to <u>androgens</u> → <u>prostatic</u> <u>hyperplasia</u> [[2]](/library/QAaujM)

* <u>Estrogens</u>: <u>Estrogens</u> (mainly <u>estradiol</u>) are potent stimulators of <u>prostatic</u> <u>hyperplasia</u>.  [[3]](/library/7Xa4zQ)

* <u>Androgen</u>-<u>estrogen</u> imbalance: As men age, <u>testosterone</u> levels decline, but <u>estrogen</u> levels remain the same, which results in a higher <u>estrogen</u>/<u>testosterone</u> <u>ratio</u>.

* <u>Stem cell</u> <u>proliferation</u> and longevity: abnormal <u>proliferation</u> and longer <u>prostatic</u> <u>stem cell</u> life-span  [[4]](/library/HXaKzQ)[[5]](/library/sXatzQ)

* Genetic susceptibility: <u>Genes</u> involved in the development of BPH include growth factor <u>genes</u>, <u>androgen</u>-regulator <u>genes</u>, <u>apoptosis</u> <u>genes</u>, and <u>androgen</u>-regulated <u>genes</u>. [[6]](/library/gYaFoQ)





> [!TIP]
> BPH is not a <u>risk factor</u> for the development of <u>prostate cancer</u>.

---

## Pathophysiology

* The <u>prostate</u> consists of zones and lobes (see “<u>Prostate gland</u>” for more information).  

* The middle transition zone/the <u>lateral</u> and middle <u>prostatic</u> lobes (periurethral lobes) are involved in development of BPH. [[3]](/library/7Xa4zQ)

* The outer peripheral zone is involved in development of <u>prostate cancer</u>.

* A combination of hormonal factors, <u>stem cell</u> <u>proliferation</u> and genetic susceptibility → glandular and stromal <u>hyperplasia</u> in the transition zone → formation of smooth, elastic, firm <u>hyperplastic</u> <u>nodule</u> → slit-like <u>prostatic</u> urethral compression → <u>BOO</u> → <u>obstructive lower urinary tract symptoms</u>

* <u>Bladder outlet obstruction</u> leads to:

* <u>Detrusor</u> overactivity (involuntary <u>detrusor</u> contractions during <u>bladder</u> filling) → irritative <u>lower urinary tract symptoms</u> [[7]](/library/GXaBzQ)

* Weakening of the <u>bladder</u> wall → incomplete voiding → urinary stasis → predisposition to <u>urinary tract infections</u>, acute/<u>chronic urinary retention</u>, and formation of <u>bladder stones</u>

* Increased intracystic pressure while voiding → <u>detrusor muscle</u> <u>hypertrophy</u> → <u>bladder</u> trabeculation and <u>pseudodiverticula</u> formation

## Clinical features

BPH typically manifests with features of uncomplicated lower urinary tract symptoms (<u>LUTS</u>), which is a nonspecific term that encompasses symptoms of <u>bladder outlet obstruction</u> (<u>BOO</u>) and <u>bladder</u> irritation (<u>overactive bladder</u> or <u>OAB</u>).




* Irritative symptoms (storage LUTS; <u>LUTS associated with OAB</u>) [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)

* <u>Urinary frequency</u>

* <u>Urinary urgency</u> and <u>urge incontinence</u>

* <u>Nocturia</u>

* Occasionally <u>dysuria</u>

* Obstructive symptoms (voiding LUTS; <u>LUTS associated with BOO</u>) [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)

* Hesitancy

* Straining to urinate

* Poor and/or intermittent stream (not continuous)

* Prolonged terminal dribbling

* Sensation of incomplete voiding

* <u>Acute urinary retention</u>

* Additional symptoms: <u>gross hematuria</u>  [[9]](/library/FXag-Q)[[10]](/library/8XaO-Q)

* <u>Digital rectal examination</u> (<u>DRE</u>) findings: symmetrically enlarged, smooth (no <u>nodules</u>), firm, nontender <u>prostate</u> with rubbery or elastic texture





> [!NOTE]
> To remember the symptoms of BPH, think “FUNWISE”: Frequency, Urgency, Nocturia, Weak stream /hesitancy, Intermittent stream, Straining to urinate, and Emptying (not emptying completely, terminal dribbling).

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)[[11]](/library/5jXiay)




Suspect BPH in patients ≥ 45 years of age with uncomplicated <u>LUTS</u>. See “<u>Diagnostic approach to suspected prostate cancer</u>” if findings from the patient's history, the examination, or diagnostics increase suspicion for <u>prostate cancer</u>.




* Initial assessment: Determine if <u>LUTS</u> is attributable to BPH.

* Obtain a detailed <u>medical history</u> and relevant <u>physical examination</u>, including a <u>digital rectal examination</u> (<u>DRE</u>), and <u>urinalysis</u>.

* Assess for <u>features of complicated LUTS</u>.

* Instruct the patient to keep a <u>voiding diary</u>.

* Assess the severity of <u>LUTS</u> using either the <u>IPSS</u> or the <u>AUA</u>-SI scores.

* Additional diagnostics: not routinely recommended 

* Serum <u>PSA</u> level: to aid selection of <u>pharmacotherapy for BPH</u> or if detection of <u>prostate cancer</u> will alter management

* <u>Renal function tests</u> and imaging of the upper <u>urinary tract</u>: if there is clinical suspicion of renal impairment

* <u>Postvoid residue</u> and <u>uroflowmetry</u>: in patients with suspected <u>BOO</u>

* Imaging and additional <u>urodynamic studies</u>: Consider in the following instances.

* Uncertain etiology

* <u>Features of complicated LUTS</u>

* Persistent symptoms despite pharmacotherapy

* Prior to surgical treatment





### Initial assessment [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)[[11]](/library/5jXiay)




#### History and examination




* A thorough <u>medical history</u> and examination are essential to evaluate for the likely cause of <u>LUTS</u>.

* Conduct <u>DRE</u> to identify <u>prostatic</u> enlargement.

* <u>Physical examination</u> should also include assessment for other causes of <u>LUTS</u> (see “<u>Differential diagnoses of BPH</u>”).





#### Voiding diary




* All patients should be instructed to maintain a <u>voiding diary</u>.

* Includes a <u>urinary frequency</u>-volume chart and additional information

* Most useful for patients with predominantly storage symptoms, such as <u>nocturia</u> [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)





#### Assess for features of complicated LUTS [[11]](/library/5jXiay)




* Suspected <u>prostate cancer</u>

* <u>DRE</u> findings suspicious for <u>prostate cancer</u>

* Abnormally elevated <u>prostate-specific antigen</u> levels

* <u>Hematuria</u>

* Suspected <u>chronic urinary retention</u>

* <u>Recurrent UTIs</u>

* Palpable <u>bladder</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u> for <u>bladder</u> disorder (e.g., neurological disorder, <u>urethral stricture</u>)





#### Symptom severity




Assess the severity of <u>LUTS</u> with a validated self-administered questionnaire to guide management and evaluate response to therapy. There are several symptom score questionnaires. The following are some of the most widely used.




* International prostate symptom score (<u>IPSS</u>) 

* A scoring system based on the presence and severity of seven BPH symptoms in the past 30 days

* <u>IPSS</u> also estimates the effect of <u>LUTS</u> on the quality of life.

* Based on the final scores, BPH is graded as follows:

* 0–7 points: mild symptoms

* 8–19 points: moderate symptoms

* 20–35 points: severe symptoms

* American urological association symptom index for BPH (<u>AUA</u>-SI): a similar questionnaire to <u>IPSS</u> but does not assess the impact of <u>LUTS</u> severity on quality of life [[13]](/library/-VcDCY0)





![International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)](media/ot4xixrp8cs1f64hfmfcz32v.jpg)

International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[11]](/library/5jXiay)[[12]](/library/rAXfO00)




#### <u>Urinalysis</u>




* Perform for all patients with <u>LUTS</u>. [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)

* Abnormal findings may warrant further evaluation, e.g., <u>urine culture</u> to rule out a <u>UTI</u> (see “<u>Urine dipstick</u>”).  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)





#### Serum <u>PSA</u> level




* Indications (not routinely required)

* Consider if <u>prostate cancer</u> is suspected in patients with a <u>life expectancy</u> of > 10 years who are eligible for <u>prostate cancer</u> treatment, if detected (see “<u>Prostate cancer screening</u>”). [[11]](/library/5jXiay)

* To aid the selection of <u>pharmacotherapy for BPH</u>  [[11]](/library/5jXiay)[[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* Findings

* Total <u>PSA</u> > 1.5 ng/mL: suggests an enlarged <u>prostate</u> (> 40 mL)  [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)[[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* Total <u>PSA</u> > 4 ng/mL: increased likelihood of <u>prostate cancer</u>  [[14]](/library/SkXyMy)[[15]](/library/hkXcny)

* Free <u>PSA</u> levels and <u>free PSA/total PSA ratio</u> [[16]](/library/wjXhcy)

* ↑ Free <u>PSA</u> levels;  and ↑ free <u>PSA</u>/total <u>PSA</u> <u>ratio</u>: usually seen in BPH

* ↓ Free <u>PSA</u> levels;  and ↓ free <u>PSA</u>/total <u>PSA</u> <u>ratio</u>: suggestive of <u>prostate cancer</u>





> [!TIP]
> Serum <u>PSA</u> levels are not measured routinely in patients with <u>LUTS</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> A low <u>PSA</u> level does not rule out <u>prostate cancer</u>!




#### <u>Renal function tests</u> [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)[[12]](/library/rAXfO00)




* Indications (not routinely required)

* Clinical suspicion of renal impairment

* Baseline levels before surgical intervention for <u>LUTS</u>

* Findings: typically normal in patients with uncomplicated BPH





### <u>Urodynamic studies</u> [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)[[11]](/library/5jXiay)[[17]](/library/uyXpS00)




<u>Urodynamic studies</u> can help identify the predominant type of <u>LUTS</u> (i.e., <u>voiding LUTS</u> or <u>storage LUTS</u>). [[18]](/library/7ec4Zb0)




#### <u>Postvoid residual</u> (<u>PVR</u>) volume




<u>PVR</u> is a measure of <u>urinary retention</u> that can be assessed using a <u>bladder scanner</u>, abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>, or direct catheterization.




* Indications [[17]](/library/uyXpS00)

* All patients with suspected <u>BOO</u>.

* Consider before treatment with <u>antimuscarinic agents</u>.  [[11]](/library/5jXiay)

* Baseline reading prior to <u>surgery</u>

* Findings

* <u>PVR volume</u> > 50mL is usually considered abnormal  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* <u>PVR volume</u> > 300 mL may indicate <u>urinary retention</u>.  [[18]](/library/7ec4Zb0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>PVR volume</u> measurement using a <u>bladder scanner</u> is a simple and quick bedside test that can be performed by nursing staff or a physician in the clinic or in the office.




#### <u>Uroflowmetry</u> [[17]](/library/uyXpS00)[[19]](/library/3kXSny)




* Indications [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)[[17]](/library/uyXpS00)

* Consider in all patients with suspected <u>BOO</u>.

* Baseline reading before surgical or medical management to assess response to therapy

* Findings: Low maximum flow rate (Qmax) can be caused by <u>BOO</u>, <u>detrusor</u> underactivity, or an underfilled <u>bladder</u>.  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)





#### Additional studies




Consider the following in patients with <u>BOO</u> caused by BPH in whom <u>conservative treatment</u> has failed to improve symptoms.




* Pressure-flow studies and/or video <u>urodynamic studies</u>: to confirm the presence of urodynamic obstruction and determine the level of obstruction [[19]](/library/3kXSny)

* <u>Cystometry</u>: can indicate <u>OAB</u> [[19]](/library/3kXSny)





### Imaging [[18]](/library/7ec4Zb0)[[20]](/library/E4X8Oy)




Imaging in patients with <u>LUTS</u> attributable to BPH is indicated to assess <u>prostate</u> size and morphology, if the results may affect treatment selection. Imaging may also be considered to rule out differential diagnoses or to assess for complications.




#### <u>Ultrasound</u>




* Indications [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* <u>Ultrasound</u> <u>pelvis</u> (<u>bladder</u> and <u>prostate</u>): Consider prior to initiating treatment to assess the size of the <u>prostate</u> and guide the choice of therapy.

* <u>Ultrasound</u> of the upper <u>urinary tract</u>: Consider in patients with significant <u>PVR volume</u>, <u>hematuria</u>, or suspected <u>urolithiasis</u>.

* Supportive findings of BPH

* Increased total <u>prostate</u> volume

* Elevated <u>PVR volume</u> (see “<u>Urodynamic studies</u>”)  [[21]](/library/pH0Lrh)

* Evidence of <u>BOO</u> (e.g., <u>bladder</u> wall thickening, <u>hydronephrosis</u>)





#### <u>Transrectal ultrasound</u> (<u>TRUS</u>) [[20]](/library/E4X8Oy)[[22]](/library/t4XXOy)




<u>TRUS</u> is not required for the initial evaluation of <u>LUTS</u> attributable to BPH. [[18]](/library/7ec4Zb0)




* Indications

* Suspected <u>prostate cancer</u> to guide <u>biopsy</u>

* To guide pharmacotherapy  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* Prior to surgical intervention

* Supportive findings of BPH: heteroechoic enlargement of the periurethral (transition) zones of the <u>prostate</u>





![Benign prostatic hyperplasia](media/ivljgx00s2tnr6uzokmkh8gl.jpg)

Benign prostatic hyperplasia




#### <u>MRI</u> and CT <u>pelvis</u> [[17]](/library/uyXpS00)[[23]](/library/XkX9my)




* Commonly used for preprocedural assessment of <u>prostate</u> volume and localization of enlarged tissue

* <u>MRI</u> can potentially differentiate BPH from <u>prostate cancer</u>.  [[24]](/library/_Eb5yv)[[25]](/library/AEbRyv)





![Enlarged prostate gland](media/f2k8jtnq066rdx6jetujatde.jpg)

Enlarged prostate gland




> [!TIP]
> Urology referral is advised for patients with clinical <u>features of complicated LUTS</u>, as these can signify a primary <u>bladder</u> disorder and/or cancer.




> [!WARNING]
> Suspect <u>prostate cancer</u> in patients with clinical <u>features of complicated LUTS</u>, those experiencing <u>constitutional symptoms</u> such as weight loss or bone <u>pain</u> (which may suggest <u>bone metastases</u>), and those with a <u>family history</u> of <u>prostate cancer</u> or <u>BRCA2</u> mutation. [[23]](/library/XkX9my)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* Other causes of <u>prostatic</u> enlargement

* <u>Prostate cancer</u>

* <u>Prostatitis</u>

* <u>Prostatic abscess</u>

* Other causes of <u>LUTS</u> 

* <u>Bladder outlet obstruction</u>

* <u>Neurogenic bladder</u>

* <u>Detrusor</u> underactivity

* <u>Urinary tract infection</u>

* <u>Diuretic</u> use





Reference: [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[11]](/library/5jXiay)




Treatment selection should be guided by symptom severity (as determined by the <u>AUA</u>-SI or <u>IPSS</u> score) and the size of the <u>prostate</u> (e.g., on imaging or as estimated using serum <u>PSA</u> levels).




* <u>LUTS</u> causing little to no bother: Consider nonpharmacological therapy (<u>watchful waiting</u>).

* Bothersome <u>LUTS</u> attributable to BPH 

* First line: <u>pharmacotherapy for BPH</u>

* Failure of initial pharmacotherapy : <u>surgery</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with <u>acute urinary retention</u> require urgent <u>bladder catheterization</u>.




### Nonpharmacological therapy [[11]](/library/5jXiay)[[12]](/library/rAXfO00)




Nonpharmacological measures should be advised to all patients with <u>LUTS</u> attributable to BPH. <u>Watchful waiting</u> (active surveillance) can be considered as the sole management of <u>LUTS</u> causing mild to moderate symptoms in a patient with no <u>features of complicated LUTS</u>.




* Review of medications [[26]](/library/qiXCsB)

* Stop or decrease the dose of nonessential drugs that can contribute to <u>LUTS</u> (e.g., <u>opioids</u>, <u>tricyclic antidepressants</u>, <u>antihistamines</u>, decongestants).

* Alter the time of medication administration to avoid <u>LUTS</u> at inconvenient times or at night.

* Dietary advice

* Avoid excessive fluid intake before leaving the house and before bedtime.

* Limit <u>caffeine</u> and <u>alcohol</u> intake.

* For <u>polyuria</u>: Reduce overall fluid intake.

* Education about <u>bladder</u> emptying techniques, such as:

* <u>Bladder retraining</u>

* Double voiding techniques

* Urethral milking





> [!TIP]
> Nonpharmacological therapy with <u>watchful waiting</u> may be sufficient management for patients with mild to moderate symptoms and no <u>features of complicated LUTS</u>. [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)




### Pharmacological therapy [[11]](/library/5jXiay)




<u>Transurethral resection of the prostate</u> (<u>TURP</u>) is the <u>gold standard</u> <u>treatment of BPH</u>. However, pharmacotherapy can delay or even prevent the need to undergo <u>surgery</u> and should be considered as a first-line option in all patients with uncomplicated bothersome <u>LUTS</u> attributable to BPH.




#### General considerations




* Pharmacological therapy is indicated in patients with moderate to severe <u>LUTS</u> attributable to BPH.

* The choice of medication depends on the predominant symptoms, <u>prostate</u> size, and serum <u>PSA</u> levels (see “Preferred first-line options” below).

* Consider serum <u>PSA</u> level testing or a <u>TRUS</u> prior to initiation of pharmacotherapy if treatment selection is based on <u>prostate</u> size or volume. [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* Symptomatic relief can be expected within weeks (with <u>alpha blockers</u>) or months (with <u>5-ARIs</u>) after treatment initiation. [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* Life-long medication is typically required unless intolerable adverse effects develop or the patient undergoes <u>surgery</u> for BPH.





#### Overview of <u>medications for BPH</u>




| <br>Pharmacotherapy for BPH [[11]](/library/5jXiay)[[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agent | Description | Agents |
| <u>Alpha blockers</u> | <br><br>* Mechanism of action<br>Inhibition of α1-<u>receptors</u> (α1A-<u>receptors</u>) in the <u>bladder neck</u> and the <u>prostatic urethra</u> → relaxation of the <u>smooth muscle</u> of the <u>bladder neck</u> and the <u>urethra</u> → ↓ resistance to urinary outflow → symptomatic improvement<br><br>* Treatment outcome: symptom control  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br><br>* Important consideration: Can cause <u>intraoperative floppy iris syndrome</u> during <u>cataract surgery</u>  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Tamsulosin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Doxazosin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Alfuzosin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Terazosin</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> |
| 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (<u>5-ARIs</u>) | <br><br>* Mechanism of action<br>Inhibition of <u>5-alpha reductase</u> → ↓ conversion of <u>testosterone</u> to <u>DHT</u> → ↓ intraprostatic <u>DHT</u> levels → ↓ <u>prostatic</u> growth and ↑ <u>prostatic</u> <u>apoptosis</u> and <u>involution</u> → improvement of <u>LUTS</u>  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br><br>* Treatment outcomes [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br><br>* Reduction of <u>prostate</u> volume<br><br>* Decreased risk of <u>acute urinary retention</u><br><br>* Important considerations<br><br>* Long-term <u>5-ARI</u> treatment can reduce serum <u>PSA</u> levels  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br><br>* Obtain baseline serum <u>PSA</u> level before initiating <u>5-ARIs</u>.<br><br>* Adverse effects: <u>sexual dysfunction</u> (e.g., <u>erectile dysfunction</u>, decreased libido, ejaculatory dysfunction), <u>gynecomastia</u> [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Finasteride DOSAGE<br><br>* Dutasteride DOSAGE<br><br><br> |
| <u>Antimuscarinics</u> | <br><br>* Mechanism of action<br>Inhibition of <u>parasympathetic</u> <u>muscarinic receptors</u> on <u>detrusor</u> <u>smooth muscle cells</u> → ↓ muscle tone → symptomatic improvement of <u>OAB</u> symptoms; see “<u>Muscarinic antagonists</u>” [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br><br>* Important consideration: Assess <u>PVR volume</u> before initiating <u>antimuscarinics</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Tolterodine</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Darifenacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Solifenacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Oxybutynin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Trospium</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> |
| <u>Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors</u> | <br>* Mechanism of action<br>Increase in intracellular <u>cGMP</u> → ↓ <u>detrusor</u>, <u>prostate</u>, and <u>urethra</u> muscle tone → improvement of <u>LUTS</u>  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Tadalafil</u> DOSAGE<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>5-ARIs</u> are also used in the management of <u>androgenetic alopecia</u> in males




#### Preferred first-line options [[11]](/library/5jXiay)[[12]](/library/rAXfO00)




| Indications |  | Preferred agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>LUTS predominantly caused by BOO</u> | Small <u>prostate</u> (< 40 mL) and/or serum <u>PSA</u> < 1.5 ng/mL | <br><u>Alpha blocker</u>  [[8]](/library/Nec-_Y0)<br> |
| Large <u>prostate</u> (> 40 mL) and/or serum <u>PSA</u> > 1.5 ng/mL | <br><u>5-alpha reductase inhibitors</u> (<u>5-ARIs</u>)  [[27]](/library/sectZb0)<br> |  |
| Severe symptoms or an inadequate response to monotherapy | <br>Combination therapy: <u>alpha blocker</u> PLUS a <u>5-ARI</u><br> |  |
| <u>LUTS predominantly caused by OAB</u> |  | Antimuscarinic (see also “<u>Urge incontinence</u>”) |
| <u>LUTS</u> caused by mixed <u>BOO</u> and <u>OAB</u> |  | An <u>alpha blocker</u> PLUS an antimuscarinic |
| <u>LUTS</u> associated with <u>erectile dysfunction</u> |  | <br><u>Phosphodiesterase</u> 5 inhibitor  [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)<br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Antimuscarinics</u> should be used with caution in patients with a <u>PVR volume</u> > 250 mL as they can decrease <u>bladder</u> strength and potentially lead to <u>urinary retention</u>. [[11]](/library/5jXiay)[[12]](/library/rAXfO00)




### Surgical therapy




While <u>TURP</u> is the <u>gold standard</u> therapy for BPH, other techniques may be preferred depending on <u>prostate</u> volume as well as anesthesia and surgical risks.




#### Indications [[20]](/library/E4X8Oy)




* Insufficient improvement with pharmacological therapy

* Development of intolerable complications on pharmacotherapy

* BPH that is causing complications (see “<u>Complications of BPH</u>”)





#### Transurethral resection of the prostate [[20]](/library/E4X8Oy)




* Procedure [[28]](/library/PkXWLy)

* Resection of the <u>hyperplastic</u> <u>prostatic</u> tissue around the <u>urethra</u> under cystoscopic guidance using a bipolar or monopolar resectoscope

* Constant distension and <u>irrigation</u> are applied to the <u>bladder</u> using large volumes of fluid.

* Perioperative complications [[29]](/library/ykXdqy)

* Bleeding (e.g., perioperative blood loss requiring <u>transfusion</u>, <u>hematuria</u>)

* <u>Urinary retention</u> (e.g., due to clot retention)

* <u>UTI</u>

* TURP syndrome (a subtype of <u>TUR syndrome</u>): dilutional <u>hyponatremia</u> due to the absorption of the irrigant by the open <u>prostatic</u> <u>blood vessels</u>  [[30]](/library/xkXEJy)

* Late complications (<u>incidence rates</u> are shown in parentheses)

* <u>Sexual dysfunction</u>: <u>erectile dysfunction</u> (up to 32%), <u>retrograde ejaculation</u> (53–75%)  [[20]](/library/E4X8Oy)[[31]](/library/qH0Crh)

* <u>LUTS</u>: transient <u>dysuria</u>;  (up to ∼ 8%), <u>urge incontinence</u> (up to 2%)  [[29]](/library/ykXdqy)

* <u>Urethral strictures</u> (up to 4%) [[29]](/library/ykXdqy)

* Recurrent BPH: Up to ∼ 7% of patients may need another <u>TURP</u> within 8 years of the initial procedure. [[29]](/library/ykXdqy)





> [!TIP]
> The risk of developing <u>prostate cancer</u> after <u>TURP</u> remains the same as that of the general male population, as the peripheral zone (where <u>prostate cancer</u> most commonly develops) is left intact. Normal <u>PSA</u> screening protocols should be followed.




![TURP](media/ha3my6sv2vfankt2fw9374j4.jpg)

TURP




#### Other surgical treatment options [[20]](/library/E4X8Oy)




* Large <u>prostates</u> (> 60 g)

* Prostatectomy (open, <u>laparoscopic</u>, or robotic); approaches include: [[32]](/library/DzX1E00)

* Suprapubic transvesical prostatectomy: suprapubic enucleation of the <u>prostate</u> through the <u>anterior</u> wall of the <u>bladder</u> [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* Retropubic prostatectomy: enucleation of the <u>prostatic</u> tissue through a retropubic transcapsular approach [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)

* Laser enucleation of the <u>prostate</u> (LEP): holmium LEP (HoLEP) or thulium LEP (ThuLEP) [[32]](/library/DzX1E00)

* Average (31–60 g) and small (≤ 30 g) <u>prostates</u>: radiofrequency-generated water <u>thermotherapy</u>, aquablation, <u>prostatic</u> urethral lift, transurethral vaporization of the <u>prostate</u>

* Small <u>prostates</u> (≤ 30 g): transurethral <u>incision</u> of the <u>prostate</u>;  (lower risk of <u>postoperative complications</u> compared with <u>TURP</u>)  [[33]](/library/AkXRqy)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Retrograde ejaculation</u> is a common complication of <u>prostate</u> <u>surgery</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Adverse effects of <u>alpha blockers</u> include <u>orthostatic hypotension</u> (relevant for elderly patients who are <u>prone</u> to falls) and <u>intraoperative floppy iris syndrome</u> (relevant for patients who are due to undergo <u>cataract surgery</u>). [[12]](/library/rAXfO00)




> [!WARNING]
> Any elevation in serum <u>PSA</u> levels in patients receiving <u>5-ARI</u> therapy should increase suspicion for <u>prostate cancer</u>.

---

## Complications

* <u>Recurrent UTI</u>

* <u>Urinary retention</u> with <u>bladder</u> distension and <u>bladder</u> wall thickening (<u>hypertrophy</u>)

* <u>Bladder calculi</u>

* <u>Hydronephrosis</u>

* <u>Chronic kidney disease</u>

* <u>Gross hematuria</u>




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
